lesson.title: A Blueprint for Peace: Wilson's Idealistic Vision
lesson.summary: In January 1918, before the fighting had even ended, Woodrow Wilson outlined Fourteen Points as his vision for a just and lasting peace built on self-determination, open diplomacy, and a new League of Nations, an idealistic plan that would soon collide with the harsher demands of America's allies.
lesson.body:
By January 1918, American troops had been fighting in Europe for months under the mobilization effort described in earlier chapters, and Woodrow Wilson wanted to articulate clearly what the United States was fighting for beyond simple victory. He hoped a statement of principled war aims would rally support among war-weary Allied populations, encourage soldiers and civilians on all sides, and perhaps even persuade Germany and Austria-Hungary to seek a negotiated peace rather than fight to the bitter end.

On January 8, 1918, Wilson delivered a speech to a joint session of Congress outlining what became known as the Fourteen Points. Several points addressed the kind of secretive, entangling diplomacy that many blamed for dragging Europe into war in the first place, discussed in the earlier chapter on the causes of the conflict. Wilson called for open covenants of peace, openly arrived at, rejecting the secret treaties that had helped commit nations to war before their publics even understood the stakes. Other points called for freedom of the seas, the reduction of trade barriers, and a general reduction of armaments to lower the risk of future arms races.

The heart of Wilson's vision, though, was the principle of self-determination, the idea that the various nationalities trapped within crumbling multiethnic empires, especially Austria-Hungary and the Ottoman Empire, deserved the right to govern themselves. Specific points called for restoring Belgium's independence, returning the territory of Alsace-Lorraine to France, and creating an independent Poland with secure access to the sea. The fourteenth and final point proposed a general association of nations, an international body meant to guarantee the independence and territorial integrity of countries large and small alike, an idea that would soon take shape as the League of Nations.

The Fourteen Points were welcomed enthusiastically by many war-weary people across Europe, and they even influenced Germany's eventual decision to seek an armistice in November 1918. But America's own allies, particularly France and Britain, viewed Wilson's idealism with real skepticism. Having endured years of devastating losses, often fought on their own soil, French and British leaders wanted Germany punished and made to pay for the damage it had caused, not simply reintegrated into a community of nations on equal footing. That fundamental disagreement between Wilson's vision and his allies' demands would shape, and ultimately unravel, the peace settlement examined in the final chapter.
